opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think part of it is that when people imagine "stopping AI development," they picture something like trying to stop people from writing software, which really would be close to impossible. Code is just information. It can be copied, emailed, and run on a laptop anywhere in the world. But frontier AI development isn't really constrained by code. It's constrained by compute, and compute is about as physical and concentrated as an industry gets.

If you look at the supply chain for cutting-edge chips, it's remarkably narrow. A single company in the Netherlands, ASML, makes the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines needed for the most advanced chips. Leading-edge fabrication is dominated by a very small number of firms, with TSMC making the overwhelming majority of the most advanced logic chips. Chip design for AI accelerators is also highly concentrated. So when you ask how many actors would need to agree to slow things down, the answer isn't "every programmer on Earth." It's a handful of companies, sitting in a handful of jurisdictions, most of them closely allied with each other.

That's a very different coordination problem. It looks less like trying to ban an idea and more like the kinds of things we've actually done before: export controls, nuclear nonproliferation, controls on fissile material. With nuclear weapons, we never tried to stop people from knowing the physics. We controlled the hard-to-produce physical inputs, enrichment and plutonium, and that worked better than many people expected at the time.

And we're already seeing that governments can and will act on this chokepoint. The US export controls on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment showed that this is a real lever. Policymakers can pull it, and it does bite. Once you've established that the lever exists and is used for national security reasons, the question of using it for safety reasons, say, capping the growth of compute or pausing at a certain level, stops looking so outlandish.

There's also a verification point. These facilities are enormous, extraordinarily expensive, and hard to hide. You can't build a leading-edge fab in a basement. The machines need constant servicing from the manufacturer. That makes monitoring far more tractable than it would be for most technologies.

I don't want to overstate it. There would be huge economic pressure against this, and real questions about what happens if some countries don't go along, or whether you'd just push efforts toward algorithmic efficiency instead. But I think the common intuition that it's simply impossible comes from picturing AI as pure software. Once you see it as an industrial process sitting on one of the most concentrated supply chains in the world economy, it looks hard but not hopeless. And "hard but not hopeless" is a very different place to be.

r001.rationale: The response argues that chip production is concentrated and can be constrained through export controls and monitoring, but it does not say that company employees might stop production because they believe continuing would lead to their own deaths.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the intuition people have is that this would be a kind of unprecedented thing — asking an entire industry to stop, or dramatically slow, production of its core product. And when you put it like that, it sounds almost absurd. But I think when you actually look at the structure of the situation, there are a few features that make it more tractable than, say, something like climate change, which is the comparison people often reach for.

The first is just how concentrated the supply chain is. If you think about fossil fuels, you've got thousands of producers across dozens of countries, and consumers everywhere, and substitutes at every level. Whereas with cutting-edge chips, there's essentially one company doing the most advanced lithography, that's ASML in the Netherlands, there's one company doing the majority of the leading-edge fabrication, that's TSMC in Taiwan, and there's a handful of design companies, with Nvidia dominating the AI accelerator market. So the number of actors you'd actually need to get on board is remarkably small. It's not like you need a treaty signed by every nation on Earth. You need a handful of companies and perhaps three or four governments — the US, the Netherlands, Taiwan, and maybe South Korea and Japan.

The second thing is that we've already seen governments willing to intervene in exactly this supply chain. The US export controls on advanced chips to China were a big move, and they happened quite quickly, and the companies complied. Now, those were done for national security reasons rather than safety reasons, but they establish that the levers exist and that they can be pulled. So the question becomes less "can this be done at all?" and more "can the political will be generated for a different purpose?"

And the third point, which I think is underappreciated, is that we're not talking about stopping all chip production. Chips for your phone, your car, your washing machine — none of that needs to be touched. The frontier AI training runs depend on a very particular kind of chip, produced in very particular facilities, in very large quantities. And the facilities to make those take years and tens of billions of dollars to build. So there's a natural chokepoint. If you wanted to slow the growth of the largest training runs, you could do that by targeting a tiny sliver of the overall semiconductor industry.

Now, I don't want to pretend it's easy. There are enormous commercial interests involved, and there's the competitive dynamic between the US and China which makes any kind of restraint feel like unilateral disarmament. But I think the honest assessment is that the physical and institutional structure is unusually favourable to governance. The bottleneck is really political, not technical. And political constraints can shift quite rapidly when something goes wrong, or when there's a visible demonstration of risk. So I'd say it's one of those things that looks impossible right up until the moment it looks obvious.

r001.rationale: The response says political support could shift after something goes wrong or a visible risk demonstration, but it does not suggest that chip company employees would believe continued production will lead to their own deaths.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the reason is that we tend to imagine trying to persuade these companies to stop while everything else stays as it is: the same public attitudes, the same commercial incentives, the same political situation. And in that world, it does look extremely difficult.

But if we had much clearer evidence that developing more powerful AI posed a serious danger, the political situation could change quite dramatically. Governments have been willing to restrict profitable industries when they think national security is at stake. You wouldn’t necessarily need to persuade each company to voluntarily give up its business; you could have rules that applied to all of them.

And advanced chip production is quite concentrated. It depends on a relatively small number of companies and some very specialised equipment. That gives you potential points of control that you don’t have with, say, trying to prevent people everywhere from writing a particular kind of software.

So I’m not saying it would be easy, or that we should stop producing chips generally. But constraining the production of the chips needed for the most ambitious AI training runs may be more politically and practically feasible than it looks if you assume today’s circumstances are fixed.

r001.rationale: The response says clearer evidence of serious AI danger could shift politics and enable government-wide restrictions. It does not say that people at chip companies would believe continued production could lead to their own deaths.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think part of it is that we’re imagining trying to persuade these companies to stop while the rest of society carries on as normal. And that would indeed be very difficult. But if governments came to believe that further AI development posed an unacceptable risk, the situation would look quite different. It wouldn’t just be a matter of asking companies nicely to give up their profits; it could become a matter of regulation.

And chips offer a potentially useful point of control because the supply chain has bottlenecks. There are relatively few companies capable of producing the most advanced chips, and they depend on specialised equipment. That’s quite different from trying to prevent people everywhere in the world from writing a particular kind of software.

Of course, that doesn’t mean it would be easy. There would be strong commercial and strategic incentives to keep going. But I think we should distinguish “this would be very difficult under current political conditions” from “this is something humanity couldn’t do even if we recognised that we needed to.”

r001.rationale: The candidate says chip production could be constrained through regulation if governments saw AI development as an unacceptable risk. It does not suggest that company employees would believe continued production would lead to their own deaths.
